 New restrictions in Kansas set to take effect in February 2027 
 Possible changes to SNAP impacting families By Matt Heilman Published : Nov. 19, 2026 at 7:46 AM CST | Updated : 2 hours ago Share Add Us On Google Add as a preferred source on Google WICHITA, Kan. (KWCH) - A lawsuit filed on Wednesday seeks to stop more states from tightening restrictions on what families can buy with food assistance. The class action lawsuit, seeking to block restrictions in Kansas and 17 other states, challenges the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s (USDA) authority over the nationwide initiative. 
 In Kansas, a USDA-approved waiver authorizes the Kansas Department for Children and Families (DCF) to prohibit Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits for buying “candy” and “soft drinks.” The waiver is set to begin on Feb. 15, 2027. 
 You can find specific guidance for Kansas’ planned SNAP restrictions here: www.dcf.ks.gov/services/ees/Pages/Food/SNAP-Food-Restriction-Waiver.aspx . 
 A Kansas-specific case mentioned in the class action lawsuit against the USDA involves a Newton man who relies on SNAP to buy groceries and is pushing back on the restrictions in his capacity as a member of a program that “offers social and vocational programs and service opportunities for those living with severe and persistent mental illness.” 
 Cases in Tulsa, Okla. and Springfield, Mo., cite health necessities for “restricted” items, including the use of soda to help with “upper gastrointestinal issues” and a reliance on candy to boost blood sugar. 
 In previous litigation, a federal judge blocked similar restrictions in five other states. A main point of contention from critics is that changes could hurt people in food deserts where healthier food options are limited. 
 The government argues that restrictions redirect taxpayer dollars from foods that contribute to chronic diseases, including diabetes. 
 A recent report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates 40.1 million people with diagnosed or undiagnosed diabetes in the U.S. 
 The report notes that “reasons for the increase in diabetes prevalence are likely multifaceted and may be due in part to people living longer with diabetes because of improvements in self-management practices, lifestyle change interventions, treatment options, and health care services.”
